```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

mod_data <- fromJSON("lower_mississippi.json5", simplifyVector = FALSE)
sett_data <- fromJSON("lower_mississippi_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- fromJSON("lower_mississippi_source_ledger.json5", simplifyVector = FALSE)
diag_na <- fromJSON("../../_shared/sites_northern_america/config/kriging_diagnostics.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

sum_pop <- function (yr) {
  sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function (r) as.numeric(r$population[[as.character(yr)]]), numeric(1)))
}

sum_bounds <- function (yr) {
  lo <- sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function (r) as.numeric(r$population_bounds[[as.character(yr)]][[1]]), numeric(1)))
  hi <- sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function (r) as.numeric(r$population_bounds[[as.character(yr)]][[2]]), numeric(1)))
  paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(lo), " to ", viscount_fmt_pop(hi))
}

reg_pop <- function (rk, yr) {
  viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$regions[[rk]]$population[[as.character(yr)]])
}

reg_bounds <- function (rk, yr) {
  b <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]$population_bounds[[as.character(yr)]]
  paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(b[[1]]), " to ", viscount_fmt_pop(b[[2]]))
}

fmt_yr <- function (y) {
  if (y < 0) paste0(abs(y), "BC") else paste0(y, "AD")
}

clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("Existing Verified ", "", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("&", "and", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub(" / ", " and ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
}
```

# Abstract

This study reconstructs the Holocene demographic trajectory of the Lower Mississippi Hydrological Unit (USGS HU 08) across 250.401 km² (3.589 five-arcminute cells) from 10000BC to 1600AD. Linking radiocarbon summed probability distributions (N = 828, median peak 1177AD) [@kelly2025] with Middle-Late Archaic earthwork surveys [@saunders1997; @gibson2000], Coles Creek, Plaquemine and Mississippian town excavations [@morse1983; @williams1983; @brain1989; @neitzel1965] and sixteenth-century Spanish expedition records [@hudson1997], HU 08 is divided into three sub-regions encompassing 107 catalogued settlements (292 dated observations) out of 208 ledger candidates.

Aggregate basin numbers climb from 1.400 (bounds 1.288 to 1.512) in 10000BC to 104,5k by 2000BC and 188,5k (173,4k to 203,6k) at 0AD, fuelled by backswamp fishing, natural-levee gardening and monumental earthen plaza construction. Mississippian and Plaquemine intensification lifts the valley to a Holocene maximum of 326k (299,9k to 352,1k; 1,3 persons per km²) in 1200AD.

Vacant Quarter contraction along the northern delta fringe lowers totals by 17,8% to 268k in 1400AD before late Mississippian and Natchez aggregation around Parkin, Bradley, Nodena, Lake George and Emerald Mound restores numbers to 276k (253,9k to 298,1k) in 1500AD [@morse1983; @cobb2002]. Following Hernando de Soto's 1541 to 1543AD campaign and introduced Old World diseases, basin population contracts 61,6% over the sixteenth century to 180k in 1550AD and 106k (97,5k to 114,5k) by 1600AD [@hudson1997; @jones2014].

# Background

The Lower Mississippi alluvial valley runs nearly a thousand kilometres south from the Ohio confluence across the St. Francis, Yazoo, Tensas-Boeuf, Ouachita and Atchafalaya floodplains to the Mississippi Birdfoot Delta. Bounded on the east by loess bluffs and on the west by Macon Ridge, Crowley's Ridge and the Ouachita terraces, this immense meander belt paired rich natural levees and oxbow lakes with the continent's densest flyway waterfowl corridors.

Unlike the broad upland Piedmont of the Southeast or the semi-arid grasslands of the Southern Plains, settlement in HU 08 clung tightly to elevated natural levees, braided-stream terraces and bluff edges above seasonal floodwaters. Those linear strips of well-drained silt loam yielded extraordinary aquatic and wild plant harvests, enabling communities along the Ouachita and Bayou Macon ridges to raise monumental earthen mound complexes at Watson Brake around 3400BC [@saunders1997] and Poverty Point around 1500BC [@gibson2000] two millennia before maize became a staple crop.

Across 828 cleaned radiocarbon dates in HU 08, Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] identify a median summed probability peak at 1177AD, matching the rise of major twelfth-century Plaquemine and Mississippian mound centres at Winterville, Lake George, Towosahgy and Lilbourn [@brain1989; @williams1983]. After 1300AD, however, regional trajectories split: northern borderlands around Cairo and the confluence margin suffered partial Vacant Quarter abandonment [@cobb2002], whereas palisaded chiefdoms in the St. Francis and Memphis corridors (Casqui at Parkin and Pacaha at Nodena and Bradley) alongside the Natchez bluffs maintained dense fortified towns into the 1540s [@morse1983; @neitzel1965; @hudson1997].

Alluvial geomorphology poses a persistent challenge across this valley. Meander migration and thick Holocene overbank siltation continually buried low-lying Early and Middle Archaic shell middens and channel-edge earthworks across the floodplain [@saunders1997; @gibson2000]. Separating genuine Pleistocene-Holocene population growth from geomorphic burial bias requires explicit spatial priors that balance excavated bluff-top earthworks against under-sampled backswamp basins [@milner2010].

```{r tbl-subregion-profiles, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
reg_names <- c(
  "St. Francis, Reelfoot and Lower Arkansas",
  "Yazoo, Tensas-Boeuf and Ouachita",
  "Natchez Bluffs, Atchafalaya and Delta"
)
df_regprof <- data.frame(
  Division = reg_names,
  Area = vapply(reg_keys, function (rk) paste0(viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$regions[[rk]]$area_km2, 0L), " km²"), character(1)),
  Pixels = vapply(reg_keys, function (rk) viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$regions[[rk]]$pixel_count, 0L), character(1)),
  Sites = vapply(reg_keys, function (rk) viscount_fmt_number(ledger_data$saturation_audit$submask_coverage[[rk]], 0L), character(1)),
  Peak1200 = vapply(reg_keys, function (rk) reg_pop(rk, 1200), character(1)),
  End1600 = vapply(reg_keys, function (rk) reg_pop(rk, 1600), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_regprof) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_regprof,
  "Sub-regional divisions of Lower Mississippi (HU 08) showing areal coverage, five-arcminute cells, catalogued settlements and 1200AD to 1600AD population benchmarks.",
  c("Sub-region", "Area", "Cells", "Sites", "1200AD", "1600AD"),
  list(label = "tab:lm-subregion-profiles", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Methodology

## Radiocarbon Kriging and Sub-Regional Partitioning

Rural spatial suitability across HU 08 derives from the continental North American non-stationary Matérn composite, which combines global radiocarbon syntheses (p3k14c [@bird2022p3k14c] and c14bazAAR) with Lower 48 state site inventories, CRM registers and CENTAUR monument records [@kelly2022; @kelly2025; @crema2021]. Following spatial and chronological deduplication across 200-year bins over 18,56M km² (18.561.382 km² across 493.687 valid terrestrial 5-arcminute cells, with 78.938 to 149.138 active inhabited non-wasteland cells per horizon), the continental domain encompasses 93.129 unique site-period observations (286.193 horizon site records) across 3.833 domestic Voronoi catchments covering 15,52M km² (15.517.268 km²; 2.570 active inhabited catchments, or 67,05%; equivalent circular radius median 29,48 km and 90th percentile 40,95 km overall, 29,3 km and 39,85 km across active catchments), achieving a 14,24x density multiplier over the 6.539-entry baseline global compilation.

Across ten horizons from 13000BC to 1650AD, 2D Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging links Freeman-Tukey transformed catchment counts to biophysical covariates capturing fluvial distance decay, coastal proximity and terrain slope. Across the outer continental and Gulf perimeter, 251 cross-frontier buffer catchments extending up to 300 km condition adjacent coastal and border margins so deltaic flanks remain free of edge bias.

Within HU 08, 3.589 five-arcminute land cells (250.401 km²) divide into three contiguous sub-regional masks (Table \ref{tab:lm-subregion-profiles}):

1. **St. Francis Basin, Reelfoot and Lower White-Arkansas Delta** (74.813 km², 29,9% of area, 1.072 cells, 34 catalogued sites): spans the Cairo-Kentucky confluence, Reelfoot lowlands, St. Francis sunk lands, Memphis bluffs and Lower Arkansas-White alluvial plains, anchoring Sloan, Pinson Mounds, Wickliffe Mounds, Towosahgy, Lilbourn, Carson Mounds, Parkin, Bradley, Nodena and Menard-Hodges.
2. **Yazoo Basin, Tensas-Boeuf and Ouachita Ridges** (102.096 km², 40,8% of area, 1.425 cells, 48 catalogued sites): covers the Yazoo-Sunflower meander belts, Macon Ridge, Tensas-Boeuf basins and Ouachita terraces, enclosing Watson Brake, Poverty Point, Jaketown, Marksville, Crooks, Troyville, Greenhouse, Winterville, Lake George, Carson Mounds Mega-Town and Parchman Place.
3. **Natchez Bluffs Southern Margin, Atchafalaya and Birdfoot Delta** (73.492 km², 29,3% of area, 1.092 cells, 25 catalogued sites): takes in the Natchez loess bluffs, Baton Rouge-Lower Mississippi deltaic plain, Atchafalaya backswamps and Bayou Teche coastal marsh ridges, containing Avery Island, Monte Sano, LSU Campus Mounds, Tchefuncte, Feltus, Morgan, Emerald Mound, Fatherland, Anna, Mazique and Medora-Houma.

## Floodplain Calibration and Uncertainty Bounds

Benchmark trajectories at 23 intervals from 10000BC to 1600AD weight natural-levee arable capacity (3 to 5 persons per km² along prime Mississippian and Plaquemine meander ridges), Archaic earthwork labour catchments and sixteenth-century chronicler counts against extensive seasonally flooded backswamps [@milner2010; @gibson2000; @hudson1997]. Averaged over entire watershed polygons including cypress swamps and bayous, sub-regional densities reach 1,07 to 1,72 persons per km² at the 1200AD Holocene peak.

Point populations for all 107 catalogued settlements are subtracted from their enclosing sub-regional totals prior to distributing residual rural counts across the five-arcminute kriging surface, smoothed across two 5-pixel passes. Symmetric 8 per cent uncertainty intervals reflect Holocene levee burial attrition, uneven mortuary and midden preservation and the steepness of post-1541AD epidemic collapse [@jones2014; @ubelaker2006].

Bayesian chronological modelling of North American mound and copper traditions [@bebber2022refining], deterministic frequency seriation [@lipo2015a], continental radiocarbon synthesis baselines [@kelly2025; @bird2022p3k14c] and radiocarbon calibration models [@crema2021] further constrain temporal span uncertainty alongside Lower Mississippi geophysical surveys.

# Testing and Validation

All spatial, variogram, gazetteer and arithmetic audits pass pre-publication bounds as of 18 November 2026 GMT+0:

1. **Kriging Sharpness and Fit**: Across all ten horizons from 13000BC to 1650AD of the North American composite, non-stationary Matérn variograms record regularised dimensionless scale $\tau_1 = 1,35$ across every horizon (1,519 to 1,6098 raw, mean 1,5782; effective short range 45,23 km to 47,94 km, mean 47,00 km), long-range scale $\tau_2 = 2,9025$ (2,9), unregularised raw nugget-to-sill ratio 0 across all ten horizons, regularised nugget-to-sill ratio 0,04 across all ten horizons and weighted least-squares residual $R^2$ ranging from 0,9990 to 0,9992 (Table \ref{tab:lm-kriging-horizons}).
2. **Gazetteer and Ledger Reconciliation**: Out of 208 candidates evaluated in the regional ledger, 107 bounded settlements (292 dated observations) enter the active point gazetteer (34 in St. Francis-Memphis, 48 in Yazoo-Ouachita and 25 in Natchez-Atchafalaya-Delta) while 101 duplicate coordinate-alias records merged within 2 km of canonical sites (led by Emerald Mound, Lake George, Fatherland, Chucalissa, Parkin and Winterville) are consolidated without non-habitation inclusions, leaving zero unaccounted entries.
3. **Arithmetic Consistency**: Sub-regional populations sum identically to the basin headline series across all 23 benchmark dates from 10000BC (1.400) to 1600AD (106k) in Table \ref{tab:lm-benchmarks}.

```{r tbl-kriging-horizons, results='asis'}
h_keys <- c(
  "palaeoindian_early_archaic", "middle_archaic", "late_archaic",
  "early_woodland_formative", "middle_woodland_hopewell", "late_woodland_dorset",
  "early_mississippian_pueblo_ii", "middle_mississippian_pueblo_iii",
  "late_precontact_thule_oneota", "protohistoric_contact_horizon"
)
h_labels <- c(
  "Palaeoindian and Early Archaic (13000 to 6000BC)", "Middle Archaic (6000 to 3000BC)",
  "Late Archaic (3000 to 1000BC)", "Early Woodland and Formative (1000 to 200BC)",
  "Middle Woodland Hopewell (200BC to 400AD)", "Late Woodland and Dorset (400 to 800AD)",
  "Early Mississippian and Pueblo II (800 to 1100AD)", "Middle Mississippian and Pueblo III (1100 to 1300AD)",
  "Late Pre-Contact and Oneota (1300 to 1500AD)", "Protohistoric Contact (1500 to 1650AD)"
)
h_rows <- lapply(seq_along(h_keys), function (i) {
  vm <- diag_na$variogram_models[[h_keys[i]]]
  data.frame(
    Horizon = h_labels[i],
    Tau1 = viscount_fmt_number(vm$tau1_dimensionless, 2L),
    RawNugget = viscount_fmt_number(vm$raw_nugget_to_sill_ratio, 4L),
    RegNugget = viscount_fmt_number(vm$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 4L),
    R2 = viscount_fmt_number(vm$residual_r2, 4L),
    RangeKm = viscount_fmt_number(vm$effective_short_range_km, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_krig <- do.call(rbind, h_rows)
rownames(df_krig) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_krig,
  "Non-stationary Matérn variogram parameters across the ten horizons of the North American radiocarbon domain.",
  c("Horizon", "Tau 1", "Raw Nugget", "Reg. Ratio", "R²", "Range (km)"),
  list(label = "tab:lm-kriging-horizons", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
key_yrs <- sort(as.integer(names(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark)))
lbl_yrs <- vapply(key_yrs, fmt_yr, character(1))
df_bench <- data.frame(
  Period = lbl_yrs,
  StFrancis = vapply(key_yrs, function (y) reg_pop("lm_st_francis_st_memphis_parkin", y), character(1)),
  Yazoo = vapply(key_yrs, function (y) reg_pop("lm_yazoo_ouachita_poverty_point", y), character(1)),
  Delta = vapply(key_yrs, function (y) reg_pop("lm_natchez_atchafalaya_delta", y), character(1)),
  Total = vapply(key_yrs, function (y) viscount_fmt_pop(sum_pop(y)), character(1)),
  Bounds = vapply(key_yrs, sum_bounds, character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_bench) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_bench,
  "Benchmark population estimates across all 23 horizons for Lower Mississippi (HU 08) and its three sub-regions, 10000BC to 1600AD.",
  c("Period", "St. Francis", "Yazoo-Ouachita", "Delta", "Total", "Bounds"),
  list(label = "tab:lm-benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Results

## Palaeoindian Terraces to Archaic Earthworks (10000BC to 1000BC)

During the terminal Pleistocene and Younger Dryas transition around 10000BC [@holliday2016blind], braided meltwater channels swept down the Lower Mississippi trough, confining human bands to elevated salt domes, Crowley's Ridge and Pleistocene terrace flanks. Basin population started near 1.400 (bounds 1.288 to 1.512) in 10000BC and rose steadily through 3.050 in 9000BC to 6,1k in 8000BC, represented by Early Archaic cemetery and salt-dome sites at Sloan in northeast Arkansas (40 to 55 across 8500 to 8200BC) and Avery Island on the Louisiana coastal salt ridge (35 at 8500BC).

By 6000BC, modern meandering river channels replaced braided glacial outwash across the central trough, creating productive oxbow lakes, cypress backswamps and seasonal fish traps that raised valley population to 21,2k. Growth accelerated through the Middle Archaic optimum, climbing from 35,8k in 5000BC to 56,2k in 4000BC and 79,5k in 3000BC.

Along the Ouachita, Bayou Macon and Baton Rouge bluffs, Middle Archaic hunter-fishers erected the earliest dated earthen mound complexes in North America: Watson Brake (480 at 3400BC) [@saunders1997], Frenchman's Bend (240 at 3500BC), Hedgepeth (210 at 3200BC), Monte Sano (260 at 3300BC) and LSU Campus Mounds (280 at 3200BC). Rather than representing sedentary farming towns, these oval mound-and-ridge rings functioned as seasonal aggregation monuments sustained by rich wetland and riverine harvests.

By the Late Archaic pinnacle between 2000BC and 1000BC, regional population climbed from 104,5k to 143,5k as Poverty Point (1,6k at 1500BC) on Macon Ridge drew seasonal gatherings and long-distance stone exchange across hundreds of kilometres [@gibson2000]. Across the river in the Yazoo Basin, Jaketown (520 at 1000BC) anchored a dense concentration of microlithic lapidary workshops along braided-stream levees. At 1000BC, the St. Francis-Memphis division held 61k (42,5%), Yazoo-Ouachita held 48k (33,4%) and the southern delta margin held 34,5k (24%).

## Woodland Plazas to Twelfth-Century Florescence (1000BC to 1200AD)

Across the Early and Middle Woodland transition from 1000BC to 400AD, steady adoption of native seed cultivation and burial-mound ceremonialism lifted HU 08 from 143,5k to 188,5k at 0AD and 247,5k by 400AD. Coastal marsh fishers at Tchefuncte (180 at 100BC) and early Hopewell-linked civic earthworks at Marksville (1,1k at 200AD) and Crooks (380 at 200AD) anchored the southern meanders, while Pinson Mounds (850 at 200AD) and Ingomar Mounds (390 at 350AD) led the interior terraces.

Late Woodland Coles Creek and Troyville communities accelerated plaza urbanisation between 400AD and 950AD, pushing basin numbers to 275k in 600AD (1,1 persons per km²) and 298,5k in 800AD. Large flat-topped mound precincts appeared at Troyville (1,2k at 650AD) on the Black-Ouachita confluence, Greenhouse (720 at 600AD) on the lower Red River, Manny (420 at 450AD) in the southern Yazoo and Feltus (720 at 950AD) along the Natchez loess bluffs, while early coastal settlements expanded along Lake Pontchartrain and the Atchafalaya ridges.

Emergent Mississippian and early Plaquemine intensification lifted totals from 314,5k in 1000AD to 322,5k in 1100AD and the Holocene peak of 326k (bounds 299,9k to 352,1k) at 1200AD, matching Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] 1177AD radiocarbon summit (Figure \ref{fig:lm-trajectory}). At 1200AD, St. Francis-Memphis held 129k (39,6%; 1,72 persons per km²), Yazoo-Ouachita held 118,5k (36,3%; 1,16 persons per km²) and Natchez-Atchafalaya-Delta held 78,5k (24,1%; 1,07 persons per km²).

Winterville (2,4k at 1200AD) anchored the upper Yazoo meander belt alongside Lake George (1,45k in 1200AD) and Rolling Fork Mounds (480) [@brain1989; @williams1983], while Lilbourn (950), Wickliffe Mounds (880), Twin Mounds (620) and Obion Mounds (540) lined the northern Mississippi-Cairo gateway. Along the western margins, Hays Mound (440) and Paw-Paw Mounds (280) marked emergent Caddoan-Lower Mississippi frontier towns on the Ouachita terraces.

## Vacant Quarter, Late Nucleation and Post-Soto Collapse (1200AD to 1600AD)

Between 1200AD and 1400AD, HU 08 declined 17,8% from 326k to 268k (bounds 246,6k to 289,4k) as fourteenth-century cooling and riverine instability reshaped northern settlement. The northern Cairo-Kentucky-Missouri bootheel corridor experienced Vacant Quarter contraction [@cobb2002], reducing Wickliffe Mounds, Towosahgy (980 at 1300AD) and Lilbourn while Winterville faded rapidly after 1300AD [@brain1989].

Population shifted southward into larger fortified polities and bluff-top capitals. Along the Yazoo and Natchez corridors, Lake George swelled to 2,2k at 1400AD [@williams1983], Anna reached 1,25k at 1350AD and Emerald Mound rose to 2,4k at 1400AD, while Chucalissa (1,35k at 1400AD) and Carson Mounds (1,8k at 1350AD) anchored the Memphis bluffs and Yazoo headwaters.

During the fifteenth century, intense palisaded town aggregation restored basin population by 3% to 276k (bounds 253,9k to 298,1k) in 1500AD (Figure \ref{fig:lm-shares}). Along the St. Francis, Mississippi and upper Yazoo levees, Parkin (2,8k at 1500AD), Bradley (2,2k at 1525AD), Nodena (2,2k at 1500AD), Carson Mounds Mega-Town (2,2k at 1450AD), Upper Nodena (1,65k), Parchman Place (1,35k), Rose Mound (1,1k), Walls (1,1k), Barton Ranch (920) and Chickasawba (780) formed tightly spaced agricultural provinces [@morse1983]. Further south, Fatherland (Grand Village of the Natchez, 1,8k at 1500AD) superseded Emerald Mound as the principal Natchez polity alongside Mazique (760) and deltaic Medora-Houma (920) [@neitzel1965].

```{r fig-shares, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_lower_mississippi_shares.png",
  "Sub-regional demographic shares across Lower Mississippi (HU 08) from 10000BC to 1600AD.",
  "fig:lm-shares"
)
```

Hernando de Soto's 1541 to 1543AD crossing of the Mississippi into the provinces of Quizquiz, Aquixo, Casqui (Parkin) and Pacaha (Nodena-Bradley), followed by Moscoso's river descent to the Gulf, initiated sharp demographic collapse [@hudson1997; @morse1983; @jones2014]. Regional totals plunged 34,8% within a single generation to 180k in 1550AD and fell 61,6% relative to 1500AD by 1600AD (106k; bounds 97,5k to 114,5k), leaving the valley 67,5% below its 1200AD Holocene peak.

Both northern St. Francis-Memphis (112k down to 42k) and central Yazoo-Ouachita (96k down to 36k) lost 62,5% of their 1500AD population as nucleated St. Francis villages fractured and retreated. The southern delta corridor dipped slightly less at 58,8% (68k to 28k), leaving Menard-Hodges (1,2k at 1600AD), Keno Place (480 at 1550AD) and Fatherland (1,4k at 1600AD) as anchors for seventeenth-century Quapaw, Tunica and Natchez survivors [@milner2010; @ubelaker2006].

## Sub-Regional Balances and Leading Urban Centres

Comparing the three sub-regions reveals an enduring demographic hierarchy across eleven millennia (Table \ref{tab:lm-subregions}, Table \ref{tab:lm-subregion-densities} and Table \ref{tab:lm-leading-centres}). St. Francis-Memphis (74.813 km², 29,9% of basin area) consistently held both the largest aggregate population (42,9% at 10000BC, 39,6% at 1200AD, 40,6% at 1500AD and 39,6% at 1600AD) and the highest population density (1,72 persons per km² at 1200AD, 1,5 at 1500AD and 0,56 at 1600AD), driven by late pre-contact palisaded town clustering across 34 catalogued complexes in northeast Arkansas and northwest Mississippi [@morse1983].

In the north, late Mississippian towns sat within a single day's walk of each other along abandoned Mississippi meander loops and Little River levees, enabling Casqui and Pacaha chiefs to muster several thousand warriors and agricultural labourers from compact alluvial strips. Once European pathogens struck these tightly packed palisaded enclaves, crowd mortality and downstream dispersal collapsed urban centres rapidly after 1543AD, shifting surviving Quapaw villages south toward Menard-Hodges near the Arkansas mouth [@hudson1997; @morse1983].

Yazoo-Ouachita (102.096 km², 40,8% of basin area) forms the largest spatial division and holds 48 of the 107 catalogued settlements. Carrying 32,5% to 38,3% of valley inhabitants across the Holocene (35,7% at 10000BC, 38,3% at 4000BC, 32,5% at 2000BC, 36,3% at 1200AD and 34% at 1600AD), it recorded moderate unit-area densities (1,16 persons per km² at 1200AD) while hosting both the earliest Archaic mounds (Watson Brake, Poverty Point) and major Plaquemine centres at Winterville, Lake George and Carson Mounds Mega-Town [@brain1989; @williams1983].

The southern Natchez-Atchafalaya-Delta division (73.492 km², 29,3% of basin area) encompasses 25 catalogued settlements spanning Baton Rouge Archaic ridges, the Natchez loess bluffs (Feltus, Emerald Mound, Fatherland, Anna and Mazique) and Bayou Teche coastal marsh islands (1,07 persons per km² at 1200AD). Protected partially by marshland logistics and dispersed delta ridges, it proved modestly more resilient after 1541AD, rising in relative basin share from 24,6% in 1500AD to 26,4% in 1600AD around Fatherland, Medora-Houma and coastal villages [@neitzel1965].

```{r tbl-subregion-densities, results='asis'}
dens_yrs <- c(-10000L, -5000L, -2000L, 0L, 600L, 1200L, 1400L, 1500L, 1600L)
dens_fn <- function (rk, yr) {
  val <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[rk]]$population[[as.character(yr)]])
  area <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[rk]]$area_km2)
  viscount_fmt_number(val / area, 2L)
}
tot_dens_fn <- function (yr) {
  viscount_fmt_number(sum_pop(yr) / as.numeric(mod_data$total_area_km2), 2L)
}
df_dens <- data.frame(
  Period = vapply(dens_yrs, fmt_yr, character(1)),
  StFrancis = vapply(dens_yrs, function (y) dens_fn("lm_st_francis_st_memphis_parkin", y), character(1)),
  Yazoo = vapply(dens_yrs, function (y) dens_fn("lm_yazoo_ouachita_poverty_point", y), character(1)),
  Delta = vapply(dens_yrs, function (y) dens_fn("lm_natchez_atchafalaya_delta", y), character(1)),
  Basin = vapply(dens_yrs, tot_dens_fn, character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_dens) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_dens,
  "Mean population density in persons per km² across Lower Mississippi (HU 08) sub-regions from 10000BC to 1600AD.",
  c("Period", "St. Francis", "Yazoo-Ouachita", "Delta", "HU 08 Mean"),
  list(label = "tab:lm-subregion-densities", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

```{r tbl-leading-centres, results='asis'}
sett_keys <- names(sett_data)
pk_vals <- vapply(sett_keys, function (k) max(as.numeric(unlist(sett_data[[k]]$population)), na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1))
top12_keys <- sett_keys[order(-pk_vals, sett_keys)[seq_len(min(12L, length(sett_keys)))]]
reg_short <- function (rid) {
  if (identical(rid, "lm_st_francis_st_memphis_parkin")) return("St. Francis-Memphis")
  if (identical(rid, "lm_yazoo_ouachita_poverty_point")) return("Yazoo-Ouachita")
  if (identical(rid, "lm_natchez_atchafalaya_delta")) return("Natchez-Delta")
  return(rid)
}
rows_top <- lapply(top12_keys, function (k) {
  sv <- sett_data[[k]]
  yrs <- as.integer(names(sv$population))
  vals <- vapply(yrs, function (y) as.numeric(sv$population[[as.character(y)]]), numeric(1))
  pk_i <- which.max(vals)
  data.frame(
    Settlement = clean_text(sv$name),
    Division = reg_short(sv$region_id),
    Span = if (min(yrs) == max(yrs)) fmt_yr(min(yrs)) else paste0(fmt_yr(min(yrs)), " to ", fmt_yr(max(yrs))),
    Peak = viscount_fmt_pop(vals[pk_i]),
    PeakYear = fmt_yr(yrs[pk_i]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, rows_top)
rownames(df_top) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Twelve largest catalogued settlements across Lower Mississippi (HU 08) by peak population descending.",
  c("Settlement", "Division", "Span", "Peak", "Peak Year"),
  list(label = "tab:lm-leading-centres", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Limitations

Four constraints shape interpretation of the Lower Mississippi demographic series. First, aggressive Holocene meandering and metres of overbank silt across the Yazoo, St. Francis and Atchafalaya floodplains deeply bury Palaeoindian and Early Archaic land surfaces, reducing radiocarbon site counts prior to 4000BC relative to upland ridges [@saunders1997; @kelly2025]. Geophysical prospection and cultural-resource record reviews along the St. Francis and Poverty Point levees show how deeply Holocene alluvium masks pre-mound midden horizons [@defense1985dtic_ada_0ad; @defense2002dtic_ada_4c3].

Second, coastal marsh subsidence and deltaic lobe switching along the Birdfoot Delta and Barataria-Terrebonne coast drown early coastal shell middens, leaving late pre-contact littoral fishing communities under-represented in terrestrial site registers compared with interior mound complexes [@defense1993dtic_ada_19a; @defense1994dtic_ada_88a; @defense2000dtic_ada_68f].

Third, the century and a half separating Spanish chronicles of 1541 to 1543AD from French explorers La Salle, Tonti and Iberville in 1682 to 1699AD creates a textual hiatus during the steepest demographic collapse [@hudson1997; @milner2010; @jones2014]. Values at 1550AD and 1600AD are therefore anchored by ceramic-phase contractions across St. Francis, Nodena and Plaquemine assemblages rather than contemporary parish returns.

Fourth, several major northern confluence polities straddle watershed margins shared with HU 06 (Cumberland and Tennessee) and HU 05 (Ohio River), while dispersed Plaquemine hamlets across backswamp bayous lack discrete nucleated boundaries and stay embedded in the continental rural density layer [@brain1989; @cobb2002].

# Conclusion

Between 10000BC and 1600AD, the Lower Mississippi Hydrological Unit expanded from 1.400 scattered post-glacial foragers to an early Archaic earthwork cradle at Watson Brake and Poverty Point, climbing onwards to a Holocene zenith of 326k inhabitants in 1200AD.

Across five millennia of mound building, the valley operated as eastern North America's central riverine corridor, linking Gulf littoral fisheries and Red-Ouachita salt and stone networks to interior Mississippian agricultural heartlands. Even when fourteenth-century Vacant Quarter contraction thinned northern towns along the Ohio-Cairo margin, Plaquemine and late Mississippian chiefdoms rebuilt dense fortified centres at Parkin, Bradley, Nodena, Lake George, Emerald Mound and Fatherland.

Sixteenth-century expeditions and imported pathogens cut basin numbers by more than three-fifths between 1500AD and 1600AD, reducing the valley to 106k inhabitants on the threshold of French colonial contact. Combining 107 catalogued monumental and town complexes (292 dated observations) with the 93.129-observation (286.193 horizon site records) North American kriging grid preserves both concentrated levee urbanism and the wider rural floodplain base across eleven millennia.
